methodological_rigor.justification: The study builds on a well-established ρ0 cell model system and extends it with multiple in vivo models in immunocompetent (Balb/c) and immunocompromised (NSG) mice, paired with comprehensive molecular characterization: mtDNA qPCR, bulk RNA-seq, Oxygraph respirometry, DHODH activity assay, NAD+/NADH ratio, native blue gel electrophoresis for respiratory complex assembly, STED microscopy for mitochondrial nucleoids, flow cytometry for immune cell profiling, LC-MS proteomics, and in vivo coculture with mito::mKate2 MSCs for direct mitochondrial transfer visualization. DHODHKO cells were generated in three human cancer lines using CRISPR-Cpf1. Statistics use two-tailed unpaired Student's t-test and one-way ANOVA, which are appropriate for the data. Limitations: mouse in vivo experiments use n=3-6 per group, which is at the low end for tumor growth studies; statistical tests for transcriptomic heatmaps are not specified; the ρ0 AOX subline analysis relies on tumor isolates without independent biological replication; and no combination therapy experiments are reported (DHODH inhibitor + immunotherapy).

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a preclinical mechanistic study (LOE 5) that directly addresses the fundamental biology of HMT and DHODH-dependent tumor growth initiation. The identification of DHODH as a broadly required enzyme for tumor onset across three cancer types (colorectal, breast, pancreatic) provides rationale for DHODH inhibitors (leflunomide, brequinar, IMU-838) as pan-cancer therapies. The demonstration that cells lacking functional respiration recruit protumorigenic M2 macrophages, neutrophils, and MSCs mechanistically links HMT to immune microenvironment shaping. The dual angle — DHODH inhibition + HMT blockade as combination strategy — is a clinically actionable hypothesis. However, no human patient data are presented and DHODH inhibitors remain experimental in most solid tumor indications.

reporting_quality.justification: Animal experiments are conducted under Czech Animal Ethics Committee approval, with specified group sizes, endpoints, and strain information. Cell lines are confirmed Mycoplasma-free with specified testing frequency. CRISPR-Cpf1 KO constructs are described with primer sequences and Sanger sequencing verification. Statistical methods are specified with P value thresholds. RNA-seq analysis pipeline specifies software versions (HISAT2 v2.2.1, FeatureCounts v2.0.3, pyDESeq2 v0.3.5). Proteomics data analyzed with MaxQuant v2.0.3.0 with 1% FDR. Gaps: formal power calculations absent; the transcriptomic heatmaps do not report per-gene statistical significance; the in vivo coculture (mito transfer visualization) uses only 2 time points from a single mixed-cell graft experiment without stated biological replication; RNA-seq GEO accession not provided in the main text.

novelty_literature.justification: The core concept — that ρ0 cells acquire mtDNA via HMT to restore DHODH-driven de novo pyrimidine synthesis — was established in the Bajzikova 2019 Cell Metabolism paper from the same group. The novel contributions of this study are: (1) the AOX transfection model demonstrating that bypassing the need for CIII/CIV via AOX delays mtDNA acquisition by ~15 days while preserving DHODH function; (2) DHODHKO validation across three human cancer lines (HCT116, MDA-MB-231, PaTu 8902) showing complete or near-complete tumor growth suppression; (3) characterization of early protumorigenic immune cell recruitment (M2 macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils) in ρ0 and DHODHKO tumors with mechanistic link to chemokine upregulation; (4) in vivo fluorescent MSC coculture demonstrating direct mitochondrial transfer. The novelty is meaningful but incremental given the established framework from prior publications.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well-organized and builds logically from the AOX delay experiment to DHODHKO pan-cancer validation to immune cell recruitment to MSC-mediated mitochondrial transfer. The Discussion correctly contextualizes findings within the HMT and DHODH literature and identifies the therapeutic implications. The mechanistic model unifying all findings is clearly articulated. Minor weaknesses: the transcriptomic heatmaps in Figs 1C and 4C-E contain many gene symbols without individual statistical annotation; the STED microscopy quantification (supplementary) is presented without per-group sample sizes; and the writing occasionally references supplementary figures for key quantitative data that would benefit from inclusion in the main figures.

key_strengths: Elegant AOX model demonstrating that bypassing CIII/CIV via alternative oxidase specifically delays mtDNA acquisition while preserving DHODH-dependent de novo pyrimidine synthesis, providing direct mechanistic evidence for the selective requirement for CIII/CIV in tumor onset

DHODH KO across three human cancer lines (colorectal, breast, pancreatic) showing consistent tumor growth suppression or elimination, providing broad cross-cancer validation of DHODH as a widely applicable therapeutic target

Novel characterization of early protumorigenic immune cell recruitment (M2 macrophages, neutrophils, eosinophils) in ρ0 and DHODHKO tumors with mechanistic evidence of elevated M-CSF and ICAM-1 as mediators of innate immune cell chemoattraction

Direct in vivo fluorescence imaging demonstrating MSC-to-cancer cell mitochondrial transfer using mito::mKate2 reporter mice, providing first in vivo visual evidence of mitochondrial donation in this model system
key_concerns: Core concept of DHODH-dependent tumor growth via HMT was established in prior publications from the same group; this study provides validation and mechanistic extension rather than a paradigm shift

In vivo tumor growth experiments use n=3-6 mice per group, which is modest for drawing broad therapeutic conclusions across multiple cancer lines; DHODHKO tumor experiments in NSG mice lack immune context

The direct causal link between early innate immune cell recruitment and subsequent mitochondrial transfer is correlative; no functional depletion of M2 macrophages, neutrophils, or eosinophils is performed to demonstrate their necessity for HMT

No pharmacological DHODH inhibitor experiments in the in vivo setting; all DHODH loss-of-function data rely on genetic KO, limiting direct translational inference for existing DHODH inhibitor drugs (leflunomide, brequinar)
chief_reviewer.rationale: This is a mechanistically rigorous extension of the DHODH-HMT tumor initiation framework with novel AOX delay experiments, pan-cancer DHODHKO validation, and mechanistic immune cell recruitment characterization. Tier 2 reflects the multi-model experimental design, novel immune recruitment findings, and direct evidence of MSC-mediated mitochondrial transfer in vivo, while the incremental nature relative to prior work from the same group and the absence of pharmacological DHODH inhibitor in vivo validation temper a tier 1 assessment.
